student_answer: The short answer: the simple linear model usually generalizes better.  Here’s why.  A high-degree polynomial can fit the training data almost perfectly—even capturing tiny fluctuations or noise. That sounds good, but it creates a classic overfitting problem: the model learns patterns that are specific to the training set but don’t reflect the true underlying relationship. When new data arrives, those “memorized quirks” don’t hold, so prediction error increases.  A simple linear model, on the other hand, may not fit the training data perfectly, but it focuses on the dominant trend. This makes it more robust to new, unseen data. This is an example of underfitting risk—but in many real-world cases, a bit of underfitting is actually safer than overfitting when your goal is prediction.

Prioritize Recall (catch as many failures as possible): 	The cost of a "missed" failure (False Negative) is significantly higher than the cost of an unnecessary check. The Math: Minimize False Negatives.  2. Prioritize Precision (few false alarms) 	The cost of a "false alarm" (False Positive) is extremely high or disruptive. The Math: Minimize False Positives.

question_text: Propose how to extend binary Logistic Regression to 3+ mutually exclusive classes.
reference_answer: The problem requires Multinomial Logistic Regression (also known as Softmax Regression), which generalizes the sigmoid function to handle multiple classes simultaneously, or using the One-vs-Rest (OvR) approach, which trains separate binary Logistic Regression models for each class against all others.
student_answer: To extend this to K mutually exclusive classes, replace sigmoid with softmax, which generalizes it to produce a valid probability distribution over all K classes. Rather than treating each class in isolation, softmax looks at the relative magnitude of class scores. A class doesn't get high probability because its score is high in absolute terms — it gets high probability because its score is high relative to all other scores. This means the model is always making a comparative judgment, not K independent binary ones. The exponential in softmax amplifies score differences, making the output distribution sharper when one class dominates and flatter when scores are close.

student_answer: Model is too shallow or too narrow — the most common culprit. Insufficient depth means the model can only learn low-order feature interactions. Insufficient width means each layer's representation is a bottleneck. Either way, the learned function is too simple relative to the data's complexity. Wrong architecture for the data modality — a fully connected network on image data, for instance, ignores spatial structure entirely. The inductive bias of the architecture has to match the structure of the problem. Mismatches here cause underfitting regardless of model size. Over-regularization — too much dropout, excessive L2 penalty, or aggressive early stopping can actively prevent the model from fitting even the training set. Regularization is meant to close the train-validation gap, not widen it; if training loss itself is high, regularization is working against you. Optimization failure — poor learning rate (too high causes divergence, too low causes stagnation), bad initialization, or vanishing gradients in deep networks can prevent the model from converging even if it theoretically has enough capacity. The model has the capacity but cannot find the solution. Insufficient training duration — the model simply hasn't been trained long enough to converge. Less common but worth ruling out first, since it's the cheapest fix.

reference_answer: Provides valid application + correct explanation of DNN usage
student_answer: A protein's function is determined not by its amino acid sequence alone, but by the three-dimensional shape that sequence folds into. A chain of hundreds of amino acids folds into a precise, stable geometry in milliseconds inside a cell — driven by physical and chemical forces. Understanding that shape is essential for knowing what the protein does, how it malfunctions in disease, and how a drug might bind to it.Determining protein structure experimentally — through X-ray crystallography, cryo-electron microscopy, or NMR spectroscopy — can take years of work and millions of dollars per protein. As of 2020, only roughly 170,000 structures had been solved experimentally, despite there being hundreds of millions of known sequences. The gap between known sequences and known structures is the central bottleneck in structural biology. AlphaFold 2 takes a raw amino acid sequence as input and outputs the full three-dimensional atomic coordinates of the folded protein — predicting where every atom sits in space, with accuracy competitive with experimental methods. The core of AlphaFold 2 is the Evoformer block, a novel architecture that maintains two coupled representations simultaneously: a per-residue representation and a pairwise representation encoding the relationship between every pair of residues. These two representations update each other iteratively through attention operations — the pairwise representation informs how residues attend to each other, and the residue-level updates feed back into the pairwise representation. After dozens of these coupled update cycles, the pairwise representation encodes rich geometric constraints about which residues are near each other in 3D space.

student_answer: The short answer is that a simple linear model (or a low-degree polynomial) almost always generalizes better to future, unseen data.  In machine learning and statistics, this scenario perfectly highlights the Bias-Variance Tradeoff, the tension between a model being too simple to capture the underlying pattern (underfitting) and a model being so complex that it memorizes the random noise in the data (overfitting).  A high-degree polynomial has immense flexibility. If you have 20 data points, a 19th-degree polynomial can snake its way through every single point, achieving a perfect training error of zero. But real-world data is composed of two things: the true underlying pattern (signal) and random fluctuations or measurement errors (noise). A highly complex model is so desperate to connect the dots that it learns the noise as if it were a permanent rule. As a result, when you introduce new data for future prediction, the model's wild, highly mathematical oscillations will completely miss the new points. This is called high variance.  A simple linear model is rigid. It cannot physically bend to touch every single training point, meaning it will always have some error on your training set (known as bias). Because it cannot bend, it is forced to ignore the random noise. It cuts right through the middle of the data, capturing the true, broad underlying trend. So when new data points arrive, they will likely fall close to that broad trend line. The model hasn't learned the quirks of the training data, so it remains stable and reliable.

question_text: Propose how to extend binary Logistic Regression to 3+ mutually exclusive classes.

student_answer: To extend binary Logistic Regression to handle three or more mutually exclusive classes, the most effective approach is to implement Softmax Regression (Multinomial Logistic Regression). This method replaces the single Sigmoid function with the Softmax function, which calculates a raw score for each potential category and then normalizes these scores into a probability distribution where the sum of all outputs equals 1. Alternatively, a One-vs-Rest (OvR) strategy can be employed, where multiple independent binary classifiers are trained to distinguish each specific class from all other combined classes, selecting the category with the highest confidence score.

reference_answer: Use Content-Based filtering initially to generate recommendations using item metadata, then seamlessly integrate Collaborative Filtering as interaction data accumulates.
student_answer: A practical hybrid recommender can use two parallel components: Collaborative Filtering to learn from user–item interactions, and Content-Based Filtering to learn from item features such as category, text, image, or brand. For existing items, the system combines both scores; for new items with no interaction history, it relies more heavily on the content-based model. As the new item collects clicks or ratings, the system gradually increases the CF weight. This design reduces cold start while still benefiting from collaborative signals when enough behavior data becomes available.

student_answer: I propose a Weighted Hybrid Architecture  to solve the new item cold-start problem.  Phase 1 (Initial Release): When a new item is added, it lacks user interaction data, making Collaborative Filtering (CF) fail. The system will rely heavily  on Content-Based Filtering. It analyzes the new item's metadata (e.g., keywords, categories, descriptions) and recommends it to users who have historically liked similar features. It gradually incorporates Collaborative Filtering (User-User or Item-Item) to leverage actual community behavior and discover deeper latent relationships, seamlessly transitioning from a pure content-based approach to a fully hybrid model.
